2. In the application, it has been stated inter alia, that on 11-7-1994, the RAJUK leased out a plot measuring 2.00 bighas of land appertaining to plot No. 69 under section 7, Uttara, Dhaka to the RAJUK Karmachari (Bohumukhi) Samabay Samiti in short 'the Samiti' for constructing a petrol pump by lease deed No. 7017 having received 'aka 1,98,387.10 for a period of 99 years. But the above mentioned Samiti found difficulty in installing a petrol pump at its own costs. Thereafter, the Samiti entered into a renewable sub-lease agreement with the petitioner on 8-9-1997 wherein it was provided that the petitioner would install petrol pump entirely at his own costs and peril having a life span of 25 years and accordingly, made over possession to the petitioner, and it is also stated that the period of lease period shall be counted from the commencement of the operation of the petrol pump and eventually, the petrol pump was started its operation on 9-3-2000 and the petitioner has been paying rent since 9-3-2000 while the petrol pump commenced its operation without any fail and the term of the lease agreement will be determined on 8-3-2028. After obtaining trade license for installation of petrol pump and observing all the formalities, the petitioner started operation of the petrol pump incurring huge investment. It is also contended that later on, the Samiti issued a notice to the petitioner for canceling the lease agreement and thus, the dispute between the petitioner and the Samiti has been crept. The lease agreement clearly depicted an arbitral clause to settle down the dispute through arbitration proceeding. Thereafter, the petitioner filed an Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 119 of 2018 before the Court of learned Senior District Judge, Dhaka, Upon hearing, the learned Senior District Judge appointed two arbitrators and on the same date, he was pleased to direct the parties to maintain the status quo in respect of position and possession of the disputed premises. Despite the order of status quo, the Director (Administration), RAJUK issued a letter to the Police Commissioner on 13-10-2022 for deploying necessary police force on 16-10-2022 at 10-00 am in order to evict the instant petitioner from the Filing Station, M/s Cosmos Filing Station and Car Service Center. Thereafter, the petitioner was constrained to file a Writ Petition on 17-10- 2022 before this Court. Upon hearing, the Writ Court was pleased to issue Rule Nisi and stayed the operation of the letter for deploying the police force. Thereafter, RAJUK filed a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2916 of 2022 before the Appellate Division impugning the order of the High Court Division. Eventually, Hon’ble Chamber Judge was pleased to dismiss the CPLA as being not pressed and accordingly, the letter to the Police Commissioner for deploying the Police Force has lost its validity and, as such, the Rule has become infructuous. After that, on the application of the petitioner, the Rule was discharged as being infructuous. 

 3. Upon hearing, the parties and considering the backdrop of the case on 6-4-2023 this Court was pleased to direct the parties to the revisional application to maintain status quo in respect of dismantling the structure, position and possession of the disputed land as mentioned in the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 119 of 2018 for a period of 2(two) months from date and also stated therein that the order no Further prayer of the extension shall be considered and with the consent of the parties this matter was fixed for hearing on 16- 5-20D at 2-00 pm on merit and the same has been duly intimated to Ms. Tanjina Sarwar, Director (Zone-3), RAJUK through e-mail, telephonic message and her contact No, 01713046932 and also by showing Lawyer Certificate as well. Moreover, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, Mr Asaduzzaman Monir being directed by this Court communicated to Ms. Tanjina Sarwar and Chairman, RAJUK for refraining from evicting the petitioner from disputed premises Being fully conversant as to the order of this Court, Ms. Tanjina Sarwar and Chairman, RAJUK did not pay heed to the solemn order of this Court and dismantled the structure of the disputed premises and dispossessed the petitioner from the disputed premises by creating a reign of terror with the assistance of the police force and after that, the disputed premises were totally sealed off and socked and, as such, the safety and security of the movable property and other assets amounting to crores of taka in the form of octane, diesel, other liquid incendiary mineral resources and other materials such as important financial records and daily receipts detailing the income and credit receipts and outstanding balances owed to different government bodies and other private parties and all these confidential business or financial records have remained locked and in an insecure state without supervision of the applicant inside the premises from 6-4-2023 and in the meantime, the applicant has suffered loss of Taka 10 crores and every day it incurs new damage. 

 5. Mr Ajmalul Hossain QC, the learned Senior Counsel with Mr MK Rahman, Senior Advocate, Mr Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury, Senior Advocate and Mr ABM Siddiqur Rahman Khan, Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that being aware the order of this Court, the RAJUK officials did not pay heed to this and showing utter disregard to the order of this Court most illegally evicted the petitioner from the disputed premises and dismantled the structure and, as such, caused irreparable loss and injury to the petitioner and therefore, they are bound to restore the status quo ante otherwise, it will cause serious prejudice to the petitioner. Mr Hossain next submits that in a series of cases, it has been held that an order of status quo ante or mandatory injunction can be granted only to restore status quo and riot to establish a new set of things. Mr Hossain further submits that this Court may in its discretion grant an order of mandatory injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts. Mr Hossain contends that, this Court has the jurisdiction to grant the order of mandatory injunction to preserve the status quo ante in order to rectify the gross tortuous wrongs committed by the opposite parties on 6-4-2023, which were committed in violation of the orders dated 13-12-2022 and 6-4-2023 passed by this Court in the instant Civil Revision. 

 6. Mr Hossain further submits that the opposite parties by their action has interfered with the order of this Court and flagrantly flouted the order Court of justice and, as such, presenting this Court with a fait accompli and therefore/ to cure the injustice admittedly caused, the Court may restore the .status quo ante by passing an order of mandatory injunction in ad interim form; otherwise, the image of the highest Court shall be disparaged in the estimation of the society. In support of his contentions Mr Hossain has referred to the cases reported in 45 DLR (AD) 762; 4 BLC (AD) 70; 35 DLR (AD) 42; 47 DLR (AD) 6; 7 DLR 606, 1994 BLD (AD) 195. 

 7. Per contra, Mr Md Sk, hid Morshed, the learned Senior Advocate along with Mrs Ayesha Morshed, the learned Advocate and Mr Niaz Morshed, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1-3 submits that the period of lease was terminated/determined on 08-9-1998 as per law, and, as such, the Clause-P of the sub-lease agreement lost its force. In support of his contention he has referred to the case reported in BCR (1987) (AD) 172. He further submits that Arbitration Miscellaneous Case is not maintainable in the eye of law; therefore, the order passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka is liable to be set-aside. He next submits that eviction process was completed before at or before 10-30 pm and the order of the Court was communicated at 11-30 pm by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. Mr Morshed also submits that the Wirt Petition being No. 11894 of 2022 challenging the eviction proceeding was discharged earlier therefore, there is no bar to start eviction proceeding and since the eviction proceeding was completed before communication of the order of this Court, therefore, there is no apparent reason to pass any order of injunction in mandatory form. He finally submits that the Court cannot grant interim relief which is amounting to granting final report and, as such, he submits that the application is liable to be turned down in limine. 

 8. Heard the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates of both the parties. have meticulously and meaningfully read the relevant materials on record along with the applications, supplementary-affidavit to the application along with Annexures thereto and counter affidavit on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1-3 dated 4-4-2023 and also perused the convoluted question of law critically involved in this case in hand. 

 10. The learned District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 119 of 2018 was pleased to appoint two Arbitrators as per the arbitral clause as mentioned in the Clause-P to the sub-lease agreement. The petitioner challenged the aforesaid order solar it relates to appointment of two Arbitrators without giving the petitioner to nominate an Arbitrator of his choice but the Samity did not raise any question the validity of the order of the learned District Judge, The learned District Judge also passed an order of status quo in respect of disputed property till first sitting of the Arbitral Tribunal. This Court considering the backdrop of the case was pleased to pass the order of status quo in respect of dismantling the structure, possession and position of the disputed premises. 

 13. In the case of 35 DLR (Supra) it was held that mandatory injunction on interlocutory application may be granted to restore status quo and by invoking inherent power Court may issue mandatory injunction for demolition of structure. In 45 DLR (Supra) it was held that the mandatory injunction is available if dispossession had taken places during the pendency of the suit or during an order of ad interim injunction. 

 15. In 24 Halsbury's Laws of England (4th Edn.) pars 948, it is sated that a mandatory injunction can be granted on an interlocutory application as well as at the hearing, but, in the absence of special circumstances, it will not normally be granted. However, if the case is clear and one which the court thinks ought to be decided at once, or if the act done is a simple and summary one which can be easily remedied, or if the defendant attempts to steal a march on the plaintiff, such as where, on receipt of notice that an injunction is about to be applied for, the defendant hurries on the work in respect of which complaint is made so that when he receives notice of an interim injunction it is completed, a mandatory injunction will be granted on an interlocutory applications. 

 16. In the case of Dorab Cawasji Warden vs Coomi Sorab Warden at others reported in 1990(2) SCC 117, the Indian Supreme Court laid down the guidelines for granting Interlocutory Mandatory Injunctions. The relevant portion of the aforesaid judgment may read thus: 

 17. In the Case of Hammad Ahmed vs Abdul Majeed & others (Civil Appeal Nos. 3382-3383 of 2019, 9 July, 2019) the Indian Supreme Court while dealing with the issue whether art interim Mandatory Injunction can be granted in a suit, held to the effect: 

 "The balance of the case totally in favour of the applicant may persuade the court to grant an interim relief though it amounts to granting the final relief itself. Of course, such would be rare and exceptional cases. The court would grant such an interim relief only if satisfied that withholding of it would prick the conscience of the court and do violence to the sense of justice, resulting in injustice being perpetuated throughout the hearing, and at the end the court would not be able to vindicate the cause of justice. Obviously such would be rare cases accompanied by compelling circumstances, where the injury complained of is immediate and pressing and would cause extreme hardship. The conduct of the parties shall also have to be seen and the court may put the parties on such terms as may be prudent." The argument that under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Code, the Court has the jurisdiction to maintain the status of the parties on the date of filing of the suit or on the date of passing of the order but cannot direct the parties to do something which was not in existence at the time of filing of the suit, is not a general rule of universal application. The nature of the orders claimed by the Appellant are not passed ordinarily in a routine manner as the Plaintiff is required to have a case which should be of higher standard than mere prime facie case." 

 18. In the case of Babul Kanti Das vs Abul Hashem", reported in 47 DLR (AD) 6 it was observed— 

 "It does not appear from the facts and circumstances of the case that the matter is purely a concern between the private rights of two parties. The matter assumed a new character and it turned into a matter concerning public policy relating to administration of justice. This Court decided in the case of Abdul laid Munshi vs Abu Bakar Siddique, 35 DLR (AD) 42 at para 12 that If a party to a suit does an Act to bring about a change in the state of things existing at the date of the suit or just prior to that date, in Order to forestall a possible Order of the court, the Court may, in an appropriate case, in exercise of its inherent power, require the offending party, by issuing a temporary injunction in mandatory form to restore the status quo ante. "We held that this principle is in consonance with fair administration of justice and this power of making an Order of mandatory injunction on an interlocutory application may be exercised irrespective of the merits of the main case as it is one of the main concerns of a Court of Law to see that no one dares to interfere with the course of justice by presenting the Court with a fail accompli." In so holding we relied upon two English cases, namely, Daniel vs Ferguson (7891)2 Ch. 27 and Von feel vs Hornsey (1895) 2 Ch. 774 and also upon some decisions of the then Dhaka High Court. The present case falls squarely within the perimeter of the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 42 and we find that the trial Court acted judiciously in passing the temporary and mandatory injunctions," 

 21. It appears that RAJUK officials are not respectful to the Court and they are completely oblivious as to their constitutional and legal obligation. We should not forget we are bound by law irrespective of our official post and position, subordinate to law and answerable to law whoever we may be. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the view that it is an appropriate case to grant interim relief otherwise, it would prick the conscience of the Court and do violence of justice and thereby injustice will be perpetuated and the delinquent officers will encourage to show thumbs up to the solemn order of the Court and it will further cause serious prejudice to the petitioner, In this respect whether petitioner is a year to year lessee or whether the disputed sub-lease creates any periodical lease or whether lease period has been expired these issues are immaterial in respect of disposing of this application. It cannot be denied that by exhausting due process the RAJUK or the Samiti may recover the possession of the disputed premises. So that as it may, if the Court's order is not obeyed by the responsible officers of the Government, it will surely disparage the position of the Court in the estimation of the people of the Country and thereby crying for establishing rule of law will be meaningless. 

 23. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and considering the exceptional circumstances especially the balance of the case in favour of the applicant petitioner persuades this Court to grant interim relief though it appears to granting final relief itself so that in future nobody dares to show disobedience to the Court's order.
